components.description: Motivation: PFN paradigm doesn't transfer naturally to time series

nodes.name: Forecasting models are typically dataset-specific
nodes.description: Most existing forecasting models are trained in a dataset-specific supervised manner, optimized separately for each target dataset, limiting their ability to learn a general forecasting mechanism transferable across tasks.

nodes.name: PFNs learn transferable inference from synthetic tasks
nodes.description: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs), e.g., TabPFN, learn an inference strategy from large-scale synthetic tasks generated by a prior distribution and transfer this strategy to unseen tasks, instead of training from scratch per dataset.

nodes.name: Tabular priors don't naturally capture time-series structure
nodes.description: Directly extending tabular PFN models to time series is insufficient because tabular data do not explicitly contain temporal order, dynamic lagged dependencies, or historical input-output correspondences.

nodes.name: Time-series forecasting requires joint reasoning over three structures
nodes.description: Time-series forecasting requires models to reason jointly over temporal dynamics, cross-variable structures, and sample-level historical patterns — none of which are natively present in tabular priors.

nodes.name: Modest reframed question: explicit reuse of historical input-output examples
nodes.description: Motivated by PFN-style learning but tempered by the tabular-transfer gap, the paper studies a more modest question: how can a forecasting model explicitly reuse historical input-output examples within a long time-series context?

nodes.name: Trio decomposes modeling into temporal, spatial, sample dimensions
nodes.description: Trio is proposed as a sample-aware forecasting architecture that decomposes multivariate time-series modeling into temporal attention (within-window dynamics), spatial attention (inter-variable dependencies), and sample attention (retrieval of relevant historical lookback-future pairs).

nodes.name: History treated as structured examples, not flat context
nodes.description: Rather than treating long historical context as a flat sequence, the model uses historical segments as structured examples that encode how past inputs evolve into future outcomes.

nodes.name: Not claiming a fully general PFN-style forecaster
nodes.description: The paper explicitly does not claim a fully general PFN-style forecaster; its goal is narrower — studying how historical input-output examples can be explicitly organized and reused within a forecasting model.

components.description: Strict temporal ordering of historical pairs and current window

nodes.name: Historical context reorganized into lookback-future pairs
nodes.description: Instead of treating historical context as one continuous sequence, it is reorganized into S non-overlapping historical blocks, each an explicit (lookback, future) pair, plus one current query window (Eqs. 1-3).

nodes.name: Historical pairs placed strictly before current window
nodes.description: All historical lookback-future pairs are strictly placed before the current query window to avoid information leakage, with explicit index formulas ensuring max index of any historical future segment is less than the min index of the current input (Eqs. 4-6).

nodes.name: No leakage of current target guaranteed
nodes.description: This strict ordering ensures historical future prompts are past observations relative to the current window and never contain the target future of the current input.

components.description: Patch tokenization and historical prompt construction

nodes.name: Current and historical lookback segments patch-embedded
nodes.description: Both the current input window and historical lookback segments are converted into patch-level token representations via a shared patch embedding layer (Eqs. 7-9).

nodes.name: Historical future segments preserved as patch-wise tokens, not compressed
nodes.description: Unlike compressing the historical future into a single vector, the historical future segment is encoded by a separate future patch embedding layer, preserving patch-wise structure and producing tokens that act as historical prediction prompts (Eq. 10).

nodes.name: Lightweight pre-encoders improve intra-window representation
nodes.description: Self-attention-based pre-encoders operate along the patch dimension to enhance local lookback and future-prompt representations before cross-window interaction (Eqs. 11-12).

nodes.name: Historical window tokens concatenate lookback and future-prompt tokens
nodes.description: For each historical window, encoded lookback tokens and future-prompt tokens are concatenated into a single window token tensor (Eq. 13).

nodes.name: Current window uses learnable query tokens as future placeholders
nodes.description: Since the current window's future is unknown, learnable query tokens are appended in place of future tokens, acting as future placeholders that later query historical future-prompt tokens during sample-level retrieval (Eqs. 14-15).

nodes.name: All windows stacked into a unified tensor
nodes.description: All historical window tokens and the current window tokens are stacked along the sample/window dimension into a single tensor Z(0) containing temporal, spatial, and sample-level dependencies (Eq. 16).

nodes.name: Full attention over all axes is expensive and uncontrolled
nodes.description: The constructed tensor contains three types of dependencies (temporal, spatial, sample-level); directly applying full attention over all axes jointly is computationally expensive and introduces uncontrolled interactions.

nodes.name: Alternating axis-wise attention decomposition proposed
nodes.description: This motivates a Temporal-Spatial-Sample alternating encoder that decomposes modeling into separate axis-wise attention operations, applied as an ordered composition per encoder block (Eq. 17).

nodes.name: Spatial attention models cross-variable dependencies
nodes.description: The spatial module reshapes the tensor and applies non-causal self-attention along the variable dimension, letting each variable dynamically aggregate information from other variables at the same sample and patch position (Eqs. 18-19).

nodes.name: Optional zero-gradient strategy reduces memory cost
nodes.description: For long-context supervised training, spatial attention for historical windows can optionally be computed under no-grad while only the current window is recomputed with gradient tracking, treating historical windows as contextual evidence and letting parameter updates be mainly driven by the current prediction loss.

nodes.name: Temporal attention captures within-window patch dependencies
nodes.description: The temporal module reshapes the tensor and applies causal self-attention along the patch dimension for each variable and sample, with a causal mask preventing later tokens from being accessed by earlier tokens (Eqs. 20-21).

nodes.name: Same zero-gradient strategy applies to temporal attention
nodes.description: When the optional zero-gradient strategy is enabled, historical windows are processed under no-grad in the temporal module too, while the current window is recomputed with gradients and replaces its position in the output.

nodes.name: Sample module retrieves historical input-output mappings
nodes.description: The sample module is designed to retrieve useful historical input-output mappings for the current prediction, performing patch-wise sample retrieval over future-query tokens rather than using a single CLS token.

nodes.name: Sample self-attention aggregates historical future-prompt tokens
nodes.description: Historical future-prompt tokens (excluding the current window) are extracted and rearranged so that sample self-attention is independently performed per variable and future-patch position, producing a memory bank of historical future-prompt representations (Eqs. 22-25).

nodes.name: Current future-query tokens cross-attend to historical memory bank
nodes.description: Current future-query tokens are extracted and used as the query in cross-attention against the aggregated historical tokens (keys/values), realizing history-first aggregation with current-only retrieval (Eqs. 26-27).

nodes.name: Only current tokens updated, avoiding bidirectional mixing
nodes.description: Only the current future-query tokens are updated and written back into the tensor, avoiding bidirectional mixing between historical and current windows while letting current prediction tokens selectively retrieve relevant historical patterns (Eq. 28).

nodes.name: All current-window tokens extracted and flattened
nodes.description: After the TSS encoder, all tokens from the current window are extracted and flattened per variable rather than using only a single CLS representation (Eqs. 29-30).

nodes.name: Shared linear head maps to prediction horizon
nodes.description: A shared linear head maps the flattened per-variable representation to the prediction horizon, either as a point forecast or as Q quantiles for probabilistic forecasting (Eqs. 31-32).

nodes.name: Input normalization and inverse normalization applied
nodes.description: Following common practice in non-stationary forecasting, each input sequence is normalized before tokenization using lookback-derived mean/std, with inverse normalization applied to the prediction (Eq. 33).

nodes.name: MSE (or pinball loss) used for training
nodes.description: For deterministic forecasting, the model minimizes mean squared error; for quantile forecasting, this is replaced by the standard pinball loss over all quantile levels (Eq. 34).

components.description: TS-SCM generator motivation and graph/node/edge mechanisms

nodes.name: GP-based synthetic priors define distribution over functions only
nodes.description: Unlike GP-based synthetic priors that mainly define a distribution over temporal functions, TS-SCM defines a distribution over multivariate causal dynamical systems.

nodes.name: TS-SCM specifies a directed causal graph with heterogeneous mechanisms
nodes.description: Each TS-SCM task is specified by a directed graph, heterogeneous node mechanisms, edge-level lag functions, noise processes, and optional mechanism drift.

nodes.name: Root vs. affected variable structure
nodes.description: TS-SCM samples root variables (exogenous driving processes from periodic functions, Fourier components, trends, GP-like priors, square waves, or chaotic systems) and affected variables generated by node-wise mechanisms receiving delayed parent inputs (Eq. 35).

nodes.name: Edge-level causal messages transform and deliver parent information
nodes.description: Each directed edge specifies an edge weight, optional nonlinear transform, lag function, reduce policy, and fill policy governing how information is transformed and delivered from parent to child (Eq. 36).

nodes.name: Lags defined at edge level, not by global delay matrix
nodes.description: A central design of TS-SCM is that lags are defined per edge rather than by a global delay matrix, allowing the lag to be fixed, state-dependent, history-dependent, sampled, or expression-defined (Eq. 37).

nodes.name: Push-based event calendar avoids rounding of continuous lags
nodes.description: Rather than the child pulling a parent value from a fixed past index, a push-based event calendar computes a future arrival trajectory for each parent value and schedules interpolated events at crossed integer time buckets, avoiding crude rounding of continuous lags (Eqs. 38-39).

nodes.name: Enables smooth delayed propagation under time-varying lags
nodes.description: This push-based, interpolated event-scheduling design enables smooth delayed propagation even when lag functions vary over time or state.

components.description: Cycle handling, drift, noise, and stability control

nodes.name: Zero-lag edges restricted to acyclic subgraph
nodes.description: Zero-lag edges are allowed only when explicitly specified, and the zero-lag subgraph is constrained to be acyclic so that same-time-step nodes have a valid computation order.

nodes.name: Positive-lag edges can form recurrent feedback
nodes.description: Positive-lag edges can form recurrent feedback loops, including self-loops and reverse-direction effects, because their messages are delivered to future time steps, avoiding ill-defined simultaneous cycles.

nodes.name: Piecewise mechanism drift simulates nonstationarity
nodes.description: TS-SCM supports piecewise drift modifying node parameters, global linear scales, or edge weights over time, along with Gaussian, Student-t, autoregressive, or mixture noise, to simulate nonstationary real-world systems.

nodes.name: Stability-aware graph sampling prevents unstable trajectories
nodes.description: To prevent randomly sampled recurrent systems from becoming unstable, incoming edge gains are controlled by a child-wise budget, with self-feedback edges given a stricter gain budget than cross-variable delayed edges, producing diverse yet learnable synthetic systems.

components.description: Forecasting episode construction aligning TS-SCM with Trio

nodes.name: Generated trajectories converted into forecasting episodes
nodes.description: Each generated TS-SCM trajectory is converted into forecasting episodes consisting of multiple historical lookback-future pairs and a current query window (Eq. 40).

nodes.name: Episode format aligns directly with Trio's architecture
nodes.description: This episode format is directly aligned with the three-dimensional attention architecture: historical pairs provide sample-level evidence while the current window retrieves relevant input-output mappings, making TS-SCM both a trajectory generator and a forecasting-oriented task generator.

nodes.name: Synthetic Dataset #1 tests variable temporal delay
nodes.description: In Synthetic Dataset #1, the target Y is an M-step delayed version of input X with M~U(20,60), testing whether a model can capture variable temporal delays.

nodes.name: Synthetic Dataset #2 additionally tests source-variable identification
nodes.description: In Synthetic Dataset #2, Y is an M-step delayed version of one randomly selected variable among five inputs (M~U(20,30)), requiring the model to identify both delay length and the relevant source variable, making it more challenging.

nodes.name: Standard baselines show limited performance under delayed dependencies
nodes.description: Standard forecasting baselines (TimesNet, Crossformer, TimeXer) show limited performance under both delayed-dependency synthetic settings (Table 1).

nodes.name: Sample Attention improves the base model on both synthetic datasets
nodes.description: Adding Sample Attention consistently improves the base model: MSE drops from 0.706 to 0.298 on Dataset #1, and from 1.011 to 0.644 on Dataset #2 (Table 1).

nodes.name: Larger improvement on the harder, variable-selection dataset
nodes.description: The improvement from Sample Attention is more pronounced on Dataset #2, suggesting sample-level retrieval is particularly useful when the model must infer both temporal delay and variable relevance.

nodes.name: Trio achieves best average MSE on 3 of 4 benchmarks
nodes.description: Trio achieves the best average MSE on ETTm1 (0.358), ETTm2 (0.255), and Electricity (0.164), out of four evaluated public benchmarks (Table 2).

nodes.name: Trio is not best on Weather but remains competitive
nodes.description: On Weather, Trio's average MSE (0.249) is not the best overall (TimeMixer++ achieves 0.226), but Trio remains competitive and achieves the best result at the short H=96 horizon.

nodes.name: Trio's advantage varies by dataset temporal characteristics
nodes.description: These results suggest Trio can effectively exploit historical input-output correspondences on most benchmarks, while its advantage may vary across datasets with different temporal characteristics.

nodes.name: ICTSP uses long context without explicit input-output structuring
nodes.description: ICTSP also attempts to use long historical context for forecasting but does not explicitly organize historical segments as input-output examples.

nodes.name: Trio's explicit pairing outperforms ICTSP's undifferentiated long context
nodes.description: Trio, using historical lookback-future pairs and sample-level retrieval, achieves better best performance than ICTSP on both ETTm1 and ETTm2 across different context lengths (Table 3).

nodes.name: Supports explicit structuring over merely lengthening context
nodes.description: This comparison supports the advantage of explicitly modeling historical input-output mappings rather than simply increasing the context length.

components.description: Ablation: effectiveness of Sample Attention on real benchmarks

nodes.name: Base Model defined as Trio minus Sample Attention
nodes.description: The Base Model shares all of Trio's backbone (patch embeddings, pre-encoders, temporal/spatial attention, prediction head, normalization, depth, hidden dim, training protocol) except that current future-query tokens do not retrieve historical future prompts via the sample dimension.

nodes.name: This isolates the contribution of sample-level retrieval
nodes.description: Because the Base Model and Base+Sample-Attention comparison differs only in sample-level retrieval, it isolates the specific contribution of historical input-output retrieval from all other architectural components.

nodes.name: Sample Attention consistently improves performance across horizons
nodes.description: Across all tested horizons on ETTm1 and ETTm2, adding Sample Attention consistently improves the base model, e.g. MSE from 0.512 to 0.424 on ETTm1 H=720, and from 0.294 to 0.230 on ETTm2 H=192 (Table 4).

nodes.name: Confirms retrieval helps capture long-range/delayed dependencies
nodes.description: These consistent improvements demonstrate that retrieving relevant historical lookback-future pairs helps the model capture long-range and delayed temporal dependencies.

nodes.name: Longer context generally improves performance
nodes.description: Increasing the context length generally improves forecasting performance across default input lengths of both 96 and 336, showing the benefit of longer historical contexts (Tables 5-6).

nodes.name: Optimal context length varies by dataset and input setting
nodes.description: The best context length varies across datasets and input settings: for input length 96, moderate lengths (L=1000-2000) already give strong performance with little further gain; for input length 336, ETTm1/ETTm2 peak around L=3000 before performance drops.

nodes.name: Excessive context may reduce training samples / add noise
nodes.description: Performance drops at very long context lengths may occur because longer input windows reduce the number of available training samples and may introduce redundant or noisy historical information.

nodes.name: Moderate long-context modeling is useful but not unconditionally
nodes.description: Overall, moderate long-context modeling is useful, but blindly increasing context length is not always beneficial.

nodes.name: Zero-shot setting assesses transfer potential, not full solution
nodes.description: The zero-shot experiment (train only on synthetic tasks, evaluate on real ETT benchmarks with no target-dataset fine-tuning) is explicitly framed as assessing the transfer potential of synthetic generation strategies, not as claiming a complete zero-shot forecasting solution.

nodes.name: TS-SCM achieves best MAE on all four ETT datasets
nodes.description: TS-SCM achieves the best MAE on all four evaluated ETT datasets when compared to CausalDynamics and LMC Synth synthetic generators (Table 7).

nodes.name: TS-SCM achieves best MSE on 3 of 4 datasets
nodes.description: TS-SCM achieves the best MSE on three of four datasets (ETTh1, ETTm1, ETTm2), while CausalDynamics obtains a slightly lower MSE on ETTh2 (Table 7).

nodes.name: TS-SCM provides more transferable priors in most settings
nodes.description: These results suggest the forecasting-oriented TS-SCM task construction provides more transferable temporal priors than the compared generators in most evaluated settings.

nodes.name: Advantage not uniform; different priors capture different dynamics
nodes.description: The non-uniform advantage (ETTh2 MSE exception) indicates different synthetic priors may capture different aspects of real-world temporal dynamics, so results are interpreted as encouraging rather than conclusive evidence.

isolated_nodes.name: Three input paradigms illustrated
isolated_nodes.description: Figure 1 contrasts three input paradigms: short historical input, long contextual input without distinguishing input-output relationships, and the paper's approach leveraging long context with explicit input-output correspondences.

isolated_nodes.name: Comparison baselines used
isolated_nodes.description: Trio is compared against TimeMixer++, Patch-wise Structural, TIMEKAN, MOIRAI, TimesFM, TimeMixer, iTransformer, PatchTST, and DLinear, covering Transformer-based, patch-based, decomposition-based, MLP-based, and foundation-style methods.

isolated_nodes.name: Standard train/val/test protocol and training details
isolated_nodes.description: Public benchmark evaluation follows standard train/validation/test splits from prior long-term forecasting studies, using Adam with initial learning rate 1e-4, MSE loss, early stopping on validation loss, and fixed random seeds with best-validation-checkpoint reporting.

isolated_nodes.name: Zero-shot evaluation protocol details
isolated_nodes.description: Zero-shot test instances use seven context samples (lookback 96, future 48 each), with the model predicting the next 48 steps given a length-96 target input, using average MSE as the main metric.

isolated_nodes.name: Compared synthetic generators for zero-shot
isolated_nodes.description: TS-SCM is compared against Causal Dynamics and LMC Synth as representative synthetic data generation strategies for the zero-shot transfer experiment.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work directions
isolated_nodes.description: Future work will focus on stronger zero-shot evaluation, synthetic-data realism diagnostics, efficiency improvements, and broader comparisons with temporal causal priors.

structural_reasoning: The graph follows two parallel design-to-validation arcs unified by a shared motivation. The motivation (C1: PFN paradigm doesn't transfer to time series) leads to a re-scoped goal of explicit historical example reuse (C2), realized architecturally through strict temporal ordering (C3), patch tokenization with preserved future-prompt structure (C4), and a three-way alternating encoder (C5) whose spatial (C6), temporal (C7), and sample (C8) attention modules are each individually justified, feeding a shared prediction head and training objective (C9). In parallel, the same motivation supports a second contribution: the TS-SCM synthetic task generator, whose design (C10: causal graph/node/edge mechanisms; C11: dynamic edge-level lag scheduling; C12: cycle handling, drift, and stability control) culminates in an episode format explicitly aligned with Trio's three-dimensional architecture (C13), tying the two contributions together. The experimental components (C14-C19) each validate a specific claim: synthetic delayed-dependency experiments (C14) directly validate the sample-attention design from C8; public benchmark results (C15) and the ICTSP comparison (C16) validate the overall architecture and its explicit-pairing rationale from C2/C3; the ablation (C17) isolates and re-confirms C14's finding on real data; the scalability study (C18) tests the boundary conditions of the long-context design from C3/C4; and the zero-shot transfer experiment (C19) validates the TS-SCM generator's transfer utility from C10-C13. Figure illustrations, baseline/protocol details, and future work are treated as isolated nodes since they are supporting context rather than embedded in a specific argumentative chain.
